opus-5.5.text:
I think they're actually quite different problems, even though people often lump them together under "audio."

For understanding — transcription, speech translation, answering questions about an audio clip — the main challenge is representation. You have a very long, dense signal, tens of thousands of samples per second, and you need to compress it into something a language model can reason over efficiently. What's worked well is a good audio encoder that produces a reasonably compact sequence of embeddings, plus an adapter that projects them into the LLM's space, so the model treats audio a bit like another modality of tokens, the way we handle images. Once you do that, a lot of the text model's capabilities transfer: instruction following, reasoning, multilinguality. The hard parts are robustness — noisy environments, accents, code-switching, overlapping speakers — and long context, because an hour of audio becomes a lot of tokens if you're not careful about the frame rate.

Generation is harder in some ways, because you're no longer just extracting semantic content. You have to produce something a human perceives as natural, and humans are extremely sensitive to small artifacts in speech. Prosody, timing, emotion, speaker identity, breathing all matter, and none of it is captured by the transcript. So you need a tokenizer or codec that preserves acoustic detail while staying compact enough to model autoregressively. There's a tension between semantic tokens, which are easy for a language model to predict but lose acoustic information, and acoustic tokens, which reconstruct well but are much harder to model because there are more of them and they're noisier. A lot of the interesting work is in combining the two, with hierarchical tokens or a language model predicting a coarse stream while a smaller model or a diffusion or flow component fills in the fine detail.

Evaluation is also very different. For understanding you have word error rate, translation metrics, QA accuracy, which are imperfect but measurable. For generation, the metrics are much weaker. Automated metrics correlate with human judgment only up to a point, so you end up relying on human evals, which are slow and expensive, and that makes iteration harder.

And then latency matters a lot more on the generation side, especially for real-time voice interaction. If you want a natural conversation, you need to start speaking within a few hundred milliseconds, handle interruptions, and stream output. That pushes you toward architectural choices you wouldn't necessarily make if you were only optimizing quality.

So I'd say understanding is increasingly "solved by scale plus a good encoder," with remaining work on robustness and efficiency, while generation still has more open questions around tokenization, modeling acoustic detail, evaluation, and latency. Ultimately you want one model that does both natively, so the understanding side informs how it speaks, and that's where a lot of the excitement is right now.

fable-5.1.text:
So the first thing I'd say is that these two problems look symmetric but they're really not. Understanding and generation share a lot of infrastructure, you can use the same tokenizer, the same transformer backbone, but the places where they get hard are quite different.

On the understanding side, the core challenge is compression. Audio is incredibly redundant compared to text. A second of speech at 16 kilohertz is sixteen thousand samples to convey maybe two or three words. So you need a representation that throws away the stuff that doesn't matter for the task, the exact phase, microphone characteristics, room reverb, and keeps the stuff that does. And what matters depends on the task. If you're doing transcription, you want something very close to phonetic content. If you're doing speaker identification or emotion, you want almost exactly the things the transcription model is trying to discard. So the hard part is deciding what level of abstraction your tokens or embeddings live at, and the honest answer is that you probably want several. Semantic tokens for meaning, acoustic tokens for everything else. Then the modeling question becomes how to fuse those into a language model so the model can reason about audio the way it reasons about text, rather than treating audio as a foreign appendage bolted onto the side.

Generation flips the problem. Now you can't throw anything away, because at the end you have to produce a waveform that sounds natural, and humans are brutally sensitive to artifacts in audio. We tolerate a slightly off word in text. We don't tolerate a metallic buzz or a glitch in prosody. So you're forced to model the high-rate acoustic detail that the understanding side was happy to discard. The typical approach is hierarchical: first generate coarse semantic or low-bitrate tokens that capture what is being said and roughly how, then condition a second stage that fills in the fine acoustic detail. The challenge is that errors compound across those stages, and the sequence lengths get very long. Even with a good neural codec you're looking at hundreds of tokens per second across multiple codebooks, and you have to decide whether to model those codebooks jointly, in a delay pattern, or with some factorized structure. Those architectural choices have a huge effect on both quality and latency.

And latency is where it gets interesting for me, because the thing we actually want is not generation or understanding in isolation. We want a model that listens and speaks at the same time, the way a person does. In a real conversation you're hearing the other person while you're formulating your reply, you're deciding when to interrupt, you're backchanneling. If you build understanding as one pipeline and generation as another and glue them with a text LLM in the middle, you lose all of that. You get this walkie-talkie experience where you talk, wait, listen. So I think the real frontier is unifying the two: a single streaming model that consumes an audio stream and emits an audio stream in the same time axis, with text as an internal scaffold the model can reason over. That forces you to confront both sets of challenges simultaneously, and in some ways that's clarifying, because the representation has to serve both purposes at once.

The last thing I'd add is data. For text, we had the internet. For audio, the amount of high-quality conversational speech that's actually usable is much smaller, and the long tail of accents, languages, and acoustic conditions is enormous. Generation in particular is very sensitive to the quality of what you train on. You can pretrain understanding on noisy, messy audio and it mostly helps. If you do that for generation, the model learns to produce noisy, messy audio. So a lot of the practical work is less about the architecture and more about building the data pipeline that lets you scale without poisoning the output distribution.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re quite different problems. For understanding, you want to extract the relevant information from the audio. If someone says a sentence, you want to understand what they said, but potentially also who is speaking, their tone, or what’s happening in the background. So transcription is part of the problem, but it’s not the whole problem. And you want to be robust to things like noise, accents, and different recording conditions.

For generation, you have to produce all those details. The text doesn’t specify exactly how a sentence should sound. There are many valid ways to say the same thing, with different pacing, intonation, and emotion. You need to choose something that’s coherent over time, while also getting the low-level acoustics right. Small errors can be very noticeable.

Then, if you want a conversational system, latency becomes a big constraint. You can’t wait until you’ve generated an entire response before you start speaking. You need to generate incrementally, but the way you pronounce the beginning of a sentence depends on where that sentence is going. So there’s an interesting tension between planning ahead and responding quickly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty important distinction between the two. For audio understanding, you want to extract information from the signal. If someone is speaking, you care about the words, but potentially also who is speaking, their tone, or what’s happening in the background. The challenge is deciding which information you need to preserve and which variation you can ignore.

For generation, you have to produce all of those details. There are many ways to say exactly the same sentence, and the model has to choose a voice, a rhythm, an intonation. So even if the linguistic content is correct, the result can still sound unnatural.

And then there’s the question of how you represent audio. You have a very high-resolution signal, so modeling it directly is expensive. You want a compressed representation that makes the sequence manageable, but preserves enough detail to reconstruct good audio. What makes a good representation for understanding isn’t necessarily what makes a good representation for generation.

If you want a system that can have a conversation, you also have to bring these together under latency constraints. It needs to understand while listening and start responding quickly, without waiting for an entire recording to finish. That adds another layer of difficulty.
